cues.en: Welcome.
cues.zh: 欢迎。

cues.en: Can I turn this on?
cues.zh: 我能把这个打开吗？

cues.en: Maybe?
cues.zh: 也许吧？

cues.en: Can people hear in the back? Can you guys hear me? Is the mic on? No. No?
cues.zh: 后面的人能听见吗？你们能听到我吗？麦克风开了吗？没有。没有？

cues.en: Maybe you can ask them to turn it on.
cues.zh: 也许你可以让他们把它打开。

cues.en: Maybe we can get a big, ah, there we go. Alright.
cues.zh: 也许我们能弄个大点的，啊，好了。行。

cues.en: Maybe we can get a bigger auditorium, we'll see. So welcome to CS 183 B. I'm Sam Altman. I'm the president of Y Combinator. Nine years ago, I was a Stanford student And then I dropped out to start a company. And then I've been an investor for the last few.
cues.zh: 也许我们能换个更大的礼堂，看看再说。欢迎来到 CS 183 B。我是 Sam Altman，Y Combinator 的总裁。九年前，我还是 Stanford 的学生，后来辍学去创业。过去几年我一直在做投资。

cues.en: So YC,
cues.zh: 那么，YC，

cues.en: we've been teaching people how to start startups for nine years.
cues.zh: 我们教人们如何创办创业公司已经九年了。

cues.en: Most of it's very hands on and specific to the startups.
cues.zh: 其中大部分都非常实操，而且针对具体创业公司。

cues.en: But 30% of it is pretty generally applicable.
cues.zh: 但其中 30% 是相当普遍适用的。

cues.en: And so
cues.zh: 所以

cues.en: we think that we can teach that 30% in this class. And even though that's only 30% of the way there, hopefully it'll still be really helpful.
cues.zh: 我们认为可以在本节课里教那 30%。虽然这只走完了 30% 的路，但希望它仍然很有帮助。

cues.en: We've taught a lot of this at YC already, but it's all been off the record. And this is the first time that a lot of what we teach in YC is gonna be on the record. So we've invited some of our best speakers to come and give the same talks they give at YC.
cues.zh: 我们在 YC 已经讲过很多这类内容，但一直都不公开。这次是 YC 教的很多内容第一次被公开记录。所以我们邀请了一些最好的讲者，来给出他们在 YC 做的同样讲座。

cues.en: We've now funded seven twenty companies.
cues.zh: 我们已经投资了 720 家公司。

cues.en: And so we're pretty sure that a lot of this advice is pretty good.
cues.zh: 所以我们相当确信，这里面很多建议都相当不错。

cues.en: We can't fund every startup yet, but we can hopefully make this advice very generally available.
cues.zh: 我们还没法投资每一家创业公司，但希望能让这些建议广泛可得。

cues.en: Guest speakers are gonna teach 17 of the 20 classes. I'm only teaching three.
cues.zh: 20 节课里有 17 节由客座讲师来讲，我只讲 3 节。

cues.en: Counting YC itself, every guest speaker has been involved
cues.zh: 算上 YC 自己，每位客座讲师都参与过

cues.en: in the creation of a billion plus dollar company.
cues.zh: 一家十亿美元以上公司的创建。

cues.en: So the advice shouldn't be that theoretical.
cues.zh: 所以这些建议应该不会太理论化。

cues.en: It's all been, it's all from people who have done it.
cues.zh: 这些全都来自亲身实践过的人。

cues.en: All of the advice in this class is geared towards people starting a business where the goal is hyper growth.
cues.zh: 这门课里的所有建议，都是面向那些创业、且目标是超高速增长的人。

cues.en: And eventually building a very large company.
cues.zh: 并最终打造一家规模非常大的公司。

cues.en: Much of it doesn't apply in other cases. And I wanna warn people upfront,
cues.zh: 其中很多内容并不适用于其他情况。我想先提醒大家，

cues.en: that if you try and do these things in a lot of big companies or non start ups, it won't work. It should still be interesting. I I really do think that startups are the way of the future and it's worth trying to understand them. But startups are very different than normal companies.
cues.zh: 如果你在許多大公司或非创业公司里照搬这些做法，是行不通的。但它应该还是很有意思。我真的认为创业公司代表着未来，值得去理解它们。但创业公司和普通公司非常不一样。

cues.en: So over the course of today and Thursday, I'm gonna try to give an overview of the four areas that you need to excel at in order to maximize your chances of success at a startup. And throughout the course, the guest speakers are gonna drill into all of these in more detail.
cues.zh: 所以，在今天和周四的课程里，我会试着概述你需要做到出色的四个领域，以最大化你在创业公司成功的几率。整门课中，嘉宾演讲者会深入讲解这些内容。

cues.en: So the four areas. You need a great idea,
cues.zh: 所以，这四个领域：你需要一个很棒的想法，

cues.en: a great product, a great team, great execution.
cues.zh: 一个很棒的产品、一个很棒的团队、出色的执行。

cues.en: These overlap somewhat, but I'm gonna have to talk about them somewhat individually to make it make sense.
cues.zh: 这些领域有些重叠，但我得分别谈谈，才能讲清楚。

cues.en: You may still fail.
cues.zh: 你仍可能失败。

cues.en: The outcome is something like idea times product,
cues.zh: 结果大致等于想法乘以产品，

cues.en: times execution,
cues.zh: 乘以执行力，

cues.en: times team, times luck.
cues.zh: 乘以团队，再乘以运气。

cues.en: Where luck is a random number between zero and ten thousand.
cues.zh: 其中运气是 0 到 10000 之间的随机数。

cues.en: Literally that much. But if you do really well in the four areas you can control,
cues.zh: 真的就有这么大。但如果你在能控制的四个领域做得非常好，

cues.en: you have a good chance at at least some amount of success.
cues.zh: 你就有很大机会获得至少一定程度的成功。

cues.en: One of the exciting things about startups is that they are surprisingly even playing field.
cues.zh: 创业令人兴奋的一点是，竞争环境出奇地公平。

cues.en: Young and inexperienced, you can do this. Old and very experienced,
cues.zh: 年轻又没经验，你也能做到。年长又经验丰富，

cues.en: you can do this too. And one of the things that I particularly like about startups
cues.zh: 你也能做到。而我特别喜欢创业的一点是，

cues.en: is that some of the things that are bad in other work situations,
cues.zh: 有些在其他工作场景中很糟糕的事，

cues.en: like being poor and unknown, are actually huge assets when it comes to starting a startup.
cues.zh: 比如没钱、没名气，在创业时反而是巨大的资产。

cues.en: Before we jump in on the how, I wanna talk about why you should start a start up. I'm somewhat hesitant to be doing this class at all,
cues.zh: 在讲具体怎么做之前，我想先谈谈你为什么应该创业。其实我有点犹豫要不要开这门课，

cues.en: because you should never start a start up just for the sake of doing so. There are much easier ways to get rich. And everyone who starts a start up always says, always, that they couldn't have imagined how hard and painful it was going to be.
cues.zh: 因为你不应该为了创业而创业。想变富，有远比这容易的路子。而且每个创业者都会说，无一例外，他们当初根本想象不到创业会有多难、多痛苦。

cues.en: You should only start a startup if you com... Feel compelled by a particular problem. And that you think starting a company is the best way to solve it.
cues.zh: 只有当你……被某个特定问题强烈驱动，并且认为创办公司是解决它的最佳方式时，你才应该创业。

cues.en: The specific passion should come first, and the startup second. In fact, all of the big successes we have at YC followed this.
cues.zh: 具体的热情应该排在第一位，创业公司排第二。事实上，我们在 YC 取得的所有巨大成功都遵循了这一点。

cues.en: So for the second half of today's lecture, Dustin Moskowitz,
cues.zh: 所以今天讲座的下半场，Dustin Moskowitz，

cues.en: the co founder of Facebook and Asana, is going to take over and talk about why to start a startup.
cues.zh: Facebook 和 Asana 的联合创始人，将接手来讲讲为什么要创业。

cues.en: We're so surprised by the amount of attention that this class got, that we wanna make sure we spend a lot of time on the why.
cues.zh: 这门课受到如此多的关注，让我们很惊讶，所以我们要确保花大量时间来讲"为什么"。

cues.en: Okay. So the first of the four areas, a great idea.
cues.zh: 好，四个领域里的第一个，一个伟大的想法。

cues.en: It's become popular in recent years to say that the idea doesn't matter.
cues.zh: 近年来流行一种说法：想法不重要。

cues.en: In fact, it's almost uncool to spend a lot of time thinking about the idea for a start up. You're just supposed to start, throw stuff at the wall, see what sticks,
cues.zh: 事实上，花大量时间去思考创业想法，几乎已经很不酷了。你只管开始，往墙上扔东西，看哪个能粘住，

cues.en: and not even spend any time thinking about if it'll be valuable, if it works.
cues.zh: 甚至不用花时间想它是否有价值、是否能成。

cues.en: And pivots are supposed to be great. The more pivots, the better.
cues.zh: 而且转型 supposedly 很棒。转型越多越好。

cues.en: So this isn't totally wrong.
cues.zh: 所以这并不完全错。

cues.en: Things do evolve in ways that are difficult to predict. And there's a limit to how much you can figure out without actually getting a product in the hands of users.
cues.zh: 事物确实会以难以预测的方式演变。而且，如果不真正把产品交到用户手里，你能搞清楚的东西是有限的。

cues.en: And great execution is at least 10 times more important and a 100 times harder than a good idea.
cues.zh: 而卓越的执行至少比好点子重要 10 倍，也难上 100 倍。

cues.en: But the pendulum has swung way out of whack here. A bad idea is still bad.
cues.zh: 但如今这钟摆已经偏得离谱了。坏点子终究还是坏点子。

cues.en: And the pivot happy world that we're in today feels really suboptimal.
cues.zh: 而我们现在所处的这个热衷转型的世界，实在让人感觉很不理想。

cues.en: Great execution towards a terrible idea will get you nowhere.
cues.zh: 再强的执行力，用在一个糟糕的点子上也走不远。

cues.en: There are exceptions, of course, but most great companies start with a great idea,
cues.zh: 当然有例外，但大多数伟大公司都始于一个伟大的想法，

cues.en: not a pivot.
cues.zh: 而不是转型。

cues.en: If you look at successful pivots,
cues.zh: 看看那些成功的转型，

cues.en: they almost always are a pivot into something the founders themselves wanted, not a random made up idea.
cues.zh: 它们几乎都是转向创始人自己真正想要的东西，而不是随便编出来的点子。

cues.en: Airbnb happened because Brian Chesky couldn't pay his rent, but he did have some extra space.
cues.zh: Airbnb 的诞生是因为 Brian Chesky 付不起房租，但他恰好有些多余空间。

cues.en: In general though, if you look at the track record of pivots,
cues.zh: 不过总体来看，看看转型的历史记录，

cues.en: they don't become big companies.
cues.zh: 它们并不会变成大公司。

cues.en: I myself used to believe ideas didn't matter that much,
cues.zh: 我自己过去也认为想法没那么重要，

cues.en: but I'm very sure that's wrong now.
cues.zh: 但我现在非常确定那是错的。

cues.en: The definition of the idea as we talk about it is very broad.
cues.zh: 我们这里所说的“想法”定义非常宽泛。

cues.en: It includes the size and the growth of the market. The growth strategy for the company. The defensibility strategy and so on. When you're evaluating an idea, you need to think through all these things, not just the product.
cues.zh: 它包括市场规模和增长、公司的增长战略、防御性策略等等。评估一个想法时，你需要把这些都考虑清楚，而不只是产品。

cues.en: If it works out, you're gonna be working on this for ten years. So it's worth some real upfront time to think through the long term value and the defensibility of the business.
cues.zh: 如果这事成了，你会在这上面干十年。所以值得一开始花些真正的时间，想清楚长期价值和这门生意的防御性。

cues.en: Even though plans themselves are worthless,
cues.zh: 尽管计划本身毫无价值，

cues.en: the exercise of planning is really valuable and totally missing in most startups today. Long
cues.zh: 制定计划这件事本身非常有价值，而如今大多数创业公司完全缺失这一点。长期

cues.en: term thinking is so rare anywhere,
cues.zh: 思考在任何地方都极其罕见，

cues.en: but especially in startups, that it's a huge advantage if you do it.
cues.zh: 但在创业公司尤其如此；如果你这么做，就是巨大的优势。

cues.en: Remember that the idea will expand and become more ambitious as you go.
cues.zh: 记住，随着推进，想法会扩展，也会变得更有野心。

cues.en: You certainly don't need to have everything figured out in a path from here to world domination.
cues.zh: 你当然不必把从这里走向统治世界的路径全都想清楚。

cues.en: But you really want a nice kernel to start with.
cues.zh: 但你确实需要一个好的内核作为起点。

cues.en: You want something that can develop in interesting ways.
cues.zh: 你希望这个东西能以有趣的方式发展壮大。

cues.en: As you're thinking through ideas, another thing that we see young founders get wrong all the time is that someday you need to build a business that's difficult to replicate.
cues.zh: 在你琢磨点子的过程中，我们还经常看到年轻创始人犯的另一个错误：总有一天，你得建立一个难以被复制的业务。

cues.en: This is an important part of a good idea.
cues.zh: 这是好点子很重要的一部分。

cues.en: I wanna make this point again because it's so important.
cues.zh: 我想再强调一遍这一点，因为它实在太重要了。

cues.en: The idea should come first and the startup should come second. Wait to start a startup until you come up with an idea you feel compelled to explore.
cues.zh: 点子应该排第一，创业公司排第二。等到你有了一个非探索不可的点子，再开始创业。

cues.en: This is also the way to choose between multiple ideas.
cues.zh: 这也是在多个想法之间做选择的方法。

cues.en: If you have several ideas that all seem pretty good, work on the one that you think about most often when you're not trying to think about work.
cues.zh: 如果你有几个想法看起来都不错，就选那个你在不工作的时候也最常想到的。

cues.en: But we hear again and again from founders that they wish they had waited to start a startup until they came up with an idea that they really loved.
cues.zh: 但我们一次又一次听到创始人说，他们希望当初能等到想出真正热爱的想法后再创业。

cues.en: Another way of looking at this is that the best companies are almost always mission oriented.
cues.zh: 换个角度看，最好的公司几乎总是以使命为导向的。

cues.en: It's difficult to get large groups of people to the extreme levels of focus and productivity that you need for a start up to be successful
cues.zh: 要让一大群人达到创业公司成功所需的极致专注和生产力水平是很难的

cues.en: unless the company feels like an important mission.
cues.zh: 除非这家公司让人觉得肩负着重要使命。

cues.en: And it's usually really hard to get that without a great founding idea.
cues.zh: 而如果没有一个伟大的创业构想，通常很难做到这一点。

cues.en: A related advantage of mission oriented ideas is that you yourself will be dedicated to them.
cues.zh: 以使命为导向的构想还有一个相关优势：你自己会全身心投入其中。

cues.en: It takes years and years, usually a decade, to create a great start up. If you don't love and believe in what you're building, you'll likely to give up at some point along the way.
cues.zh: 创建一家伟大的创业公司需要年复一年，通常要十年。如果你不热爱、不相信自己正在做的事，很可能中途某个时候就会放弃。

cues.en: There's no way I know of to get through the pain of a start up without belief that the mission really matters.
cues.zh: 据我所知，如果没有对使命真正重要的信念，就没法熬过创业的痛苦。

cues.en: A lot of founders, especially students, believe that their start up's only gonna take two or three years. And then after that, they'll work on what they're really passionate about. That almost never works. Good start ups usually take ten years.
cues.zh: 很多创始人，尤其是学生，以为自己的创业只要两三年，之后再去做自己真正热爱的事。这几乎从来行不通。好的创业通常要花十年。

cues.en: A third advantage of mission oriented companies is that people outside the company
cues.zh: 以使命为导向的公司还有第三个优势，就是公司外部的人

cues.en: are more willing to help you. You'll get more support on a hard, important project than a derivative one. When it comes to starting start ups,
cues.zh: 更愿意帮你。做一个艰难而重要的项目，比做一个衍生性的项目能得到更多支持。说到创业，

cues.en: in many ways it's easier to start a hard startup than an easy startup. This is one of those counter intuitive things that takes people a long time to understand.
cues.zh: 从很多方面来说，创办一家艰难的创业公司，比创办一家容易的更容易。这类反直觉的事，人们往往要花很长时间才能理解。

cues.en: It's difficult to overstate how important being mission driven is. So I wanna emphasize it one last time.
cues.zh: 使命驱动有多重要，怎么说都不为过。所以我想最后再强调一次。

cues.en: Derivative companies,
cues.zh: 衍生型公司，

cues.en: companies that copy an existing idea with very few new insights,
cues.zh: 也就是照搬现有想法、几乎没有新见解的公司，

cues.en: don't excite people and they don't compel the teams to work hard enough to be successful.
cues.zh: 无法让人兴奋，也无法推动团队足够努力去取得成功。

cues.en: Paul Graham is gonna talk about how to get startup ideas next week.
cues.zh: Paul Graham 下周会讲如何获得创业点子。

cues.en: It's something that a lot of founders struggle with, but it's something I believe you can get better with it. Better at with practice. And it's definitely worth trying to get better at.
cues.zh: 这是很多创始人都会纠结的事，但我相信你可以做得更好。通过练习可以变得更好。而且绝对值得努力提升。

cues.en: The hardest part about coming up with great ideas is that the best ideas often look terrible at the beginning.
cues.zh: 想出伟大创意最难的一点是，最好的创意起初往往看起来很糟。

cues.en: The thirteenth search engine and without all the features of a web portal, most people thought that was pointless. Search was done and anyway, it didn't matter that much. Portals were where the value was at. The tenth social network and limited only to college students with no money, Also terrible. MySpace had won and who wants college students as customers? Or a way to stay on strangers' couches. That just sounds terrible all around.
cues.zh: 第十三个搜索引擎，还不具备门户网站的全部功能，多数人觉得这毫无意义。搜索已经尘埃落定，而且也没那么重要。价值在门户网站上。第十个社交网络，只限没钱的大学生使用，同样糟糕。MySpace 已经赢了，谁想要大学生当客户？或者一种睡陌生人沙发的方式。这听起来整体上就很糟。

cues.en: These all sounded really bad, but they turned out to be good. If they had sounded really good, there would have been too many people working on them.
cues.zh: 这些想法当时听起来都很糟，但结果却很好。如果它们当时听起来很好，那做的人就会太多了。

cues.en: As Peter Thiel is gonna discuss in the fifth class, you want an idea that turns into a monopoly.
cues.zh: 正如 Peter Thiel 将在第五节课上讨论的，你要的是一个能变成垄断的点子。

cues.en: But you can't get a monopoly in a big market right away. Too much competition for that. You have to find a small market in which you can get a monopoly and then quickly expand.
cues.zh: 但你没法在大市场里立刻做到垄断，竞争太激烈了。你得先找到一个小市场，在那里取得垄断，然后快速扩张。

cues.en: This is why some great startup ideas look really bad at the beginning.
cues.zh: 这就是为什么有些很棒的创业点子一开始看起来非常糟糕。

cues.en: It's good if you can say something like, today, only the small subset of users are going to use my product, but I'm gonna get all of them. And in the future, almost everyone will use my product. Here's
cues.zh: 如果你能这样说就很好：今天只有一小部分用户会用我的产品，但我会把他们全都拿下；而未来，几乎所有人都会用我的产品。接下来是

cues.en: the theme that's gonna come up a lot.
cues.zh: 一个会反复出现的主题。

cues.en: You need conviction in your own beliefs
cues.zh: 你需要对自己的信念有坚定的信心，

cues.en: and a willingness to ignore others naysaying.
cues.zh: 还要愿意无视别人的唱衰。

cues.en: The hard part is that this is a very fine line. There's right on one side of it and crazy on the other.
cues.zh: 难就难在，这是一条非常细的界线：一边是对的，另一边是疯狂。

cues.en: But keep in mind that if you do come up with a great idea, most people are going to think it's bad. You should be happy about that. It means they won't compete with you. This is also a reason why it's not usually dangerous to tell people about your idea.
cues.zh: 但要记住，如果你真的想出了一个好点子，大多数人会觉得它很糟糕。你应该为此高兴。这意味着他们不会跟你竞争。这也是为什么通常告诉别人你的想法并不危险。

cues.en: The truly good ideas don't sound like they're worth stealing.
cues.zh: 真正好的点子，听起来都不像是值得偷的。

cues.en: You want an idea about what you can say. I know it sounds like a bad idea, but here's specifically why it's actually a great one. You wanna sound crazy, but you wanna actually be right. And you want an idea that not many other people are working on. And it's okay if it doesn't sound big at first. Common mistake among founders, especially first time founders, is they think that the first version of their product, the first version of their idea needs to sound really big. But it doesn't. It needs to take over a small specific market
cues.zh: 你需要的是一个关于自己能说什么的点子。我知道这听起来像个坏主意，但下面具体说说为什么它其实是个很棒的主意。你想听起来疯狂，但你又想实际上是对的。而且你想要一个没多少其他人在做的点子。如果它一开始听起来不宏大，也没关系。创始人常犯的错误，尤其是第一次创业的创始人，就是以为产品的第一个版本、点子的第一个版本，必须听起来非常宏大。但其实不必。它需要占领一个小的特定市场。

cues.en: and expand from there. That's how most great companies have started.
cues.zh: 然后从那里扩展。大多数伟大的公司都是这样起步的。

cues.en: Unpopular but right is what you're going for. You want something that sounds like a bad idea, but is a good idea.
cues.zh: 你要追求的是不受欢迎但正确的东西。你要的是那种听起来像坏主意、其实是好主意的东西。

cues.en: You also really wanna take the time to think about how the market's going to evolve.
cues.zh: 你还要真正花时间去思考市场将如何演变。

cues.en: You need a market that's going to be big in ten years.
cues.zh: 你需要一个十年后会很大的市场。

cues.en: Most investors are obsessed with the market size today. And they don't think at all about how the market's going to evolve. In fact, I think this is one of the biggest systemic mistakes that investors make. They think about the growth of the startup itself. They don't think about the growth of the market.
cues.zh: 大多数投资者痴迷于今天的市场规模。他们完全不考虑市场将如何演变。事实上，我认为这是投资者犯下的最大的系统性错误之一。他们考虑的是创业公司自身的增长，而不考虑市场的增长。

cues.en: I care much more about the growth rate of the market than its current size. And I also care if there's any reason that it's gonna top out.
cues.zh: 比起市场当前的规模，我更在意它的增长率。我也在意它有没有见顶的理由。

cues.en: You should think about this. I prefer to invest in a company that's going after a small but rapidly growing market than a big but slow growing one.
cues.zh: 这一点你该好好想想。我更愿意投资一家瞄准小而快速增长市场的公司，而不是大而增长缓慢的市场。

cues.en: One of the big advantages of these sorts of markets,
cues.zh: 这类市场的一大优势是，

cues.en: these small but rapidly growing markets, is that customers are usually pretty desperate for a solution. And they'll put up with an imperfect but rapidly improving product.
cues.zh: 这些规模小但增长快的市场，客户通常非常渴望解决方案。他们愿意接受一个还不完美但进步很快的产品。

cues.en: And a big advantage of being a student, one of the two biggest advantages,
cues.zh: 作为学生的一大优势，也是两大优势之一，

cues.en: is that you probably have better intuition about which markets are likely to start growing rapidly than older people do.
cues.zh: 就是你可能比年长的人更敏锐地直觉判断出哪些市场会开始快速增长。

cues.en: Another thing that students usually don't understand, or at least takes a while. You cannot create a market that doesn't wanna exist. You can basically change everything in a start up but the market. So you should actually do some thinking to be sure, or at least as sure as you can be, that the market you're going after is going to grow and be there.
cues.zh: 还有一件事学生通常不理解，或者至少要花些时间才能明白。你无法创造出一个本就不想存在的市场。在创业公司里，你几乎可以改变一切，唯独市场不行。所以你确实该好好想想，确保——或至少尽可能确保——你要进军的那块市场会增长，并且会持续存在。

cues.en: There are a lot of different ways to talk about the right kind of market. For example, surfing someone else's wave or stepping into an up elevator or being part of a movement. But all of this is just a way of saying, you want a market that's going to grow really quickly. It may seem small today. It may be small today. But you know, and other people don't, that it's gonna grow really fast.
cues.zh: 谈论“合适的市场”有很多种说法。比如，搭上别人掀起的浪、踏进向上的电梯、或者成为一场运动的一部分。但说到底，这些都是在说：你要的是一个会飞速增长的市场。它今天可能看起来很小，今天可能确实很小。但你知道、而别人不知道的是，它会增长得非常快。

cues.en: So think about where this is happening in the world. You need this sort of a tailwind to make a start up successful.
cues.zh: 所以，想想世界上正在发生这种事的地方。你需要这样一股顺风，才能让一家创业公司成功。

cues.en: The exciting thing is there are probably more of these tailwinds now than ever before.
cues.zh: 令人兴奋的是，现在这类顺风可能比以往任何时候都多。

cues.en: As Mark Andreessen says, software's eating the world.
cues.zh: 正如 Mark Andreessen 所说，软件正在吞噬世界。

cues.en: It's just everywhere. There are like so many great ideas out there. And you just have to pick one and find one that you really care about.
cues.zh: 它简直无处不在。外面有太多很棒的想法。你只需要挑一个，找到一个你真正关心的。

cues.en: Another version of this that would, gets down to the same idea is Sequoia's famous question. Why now?
cues.zh: 另一个说法归根结底也是同一个思路，就是 Sequoia 那个著名的问题。为什么是现在？

cues.en: Why is this the perfect time for this particular idea and to start this particular company?
cues.zh: 为什么现在是这个特定想法、创办这家特定公司的最佳时机？

cues.en: Why couldn't it have been done two years ago? And why will two years in the future be too late?
cues.zh: 为什么两年前做不了？又为什么两年后再做就太晚了？

cues.en: For the most successful startups we've been involved with, they've all had a great idea, great answer to this question.
cues.zh: 我们参与过的最成功的创业公司，都对这个问题有很好的答案。

cues.en: And if you don't, you should be at least somewhat suspicious about it.
cues.zh: 如果你答不上来，至少该对此有点怀疑。

cues.en: In general, it's best if you're building something that you yourself need.
cues.zh: 一般来说，最好的情况是你做的是自己需要的东西。

cues.en: You'll understand it much better if you have to understand it by talking to a customer to build the very first version.
cues.zh: 如果你必须通过和客户交流才能做出第一个版本，你会理解得透彻得多。

cues.en: If you don't need it yourself and you're building something that someone else needs, realize that you're at a big disadvantage and get very, very close to your customers. Try to work in their office if you can. And if not, talk to them multiple times a day.
cues.zh: 如果你自己并不需要它，而你做的东西是别人需要的，那你要意识到自己处于很大劣势，必须非常、非常贴近你的客户。能去他们办公室办公就去，去不了的话，一天和他们聊好几次。

cues.en: Another somewhat counterintuitive thing about good start up ideas is that they're almost always very easy to explain and very easy to understand.
cues.zh: 关于好的创业点子，还有一点有点反直觉：它们几乎总是很容易解释、也很容易理解。

cues.en: If it takes more than a sentence to explain what you're doing, it's almost always a sign that it's too complicated.
cues.zh: 如果要花超过一句话来解释你在做什么，这几乎总是说明它太复杂了。

cues.en: It should be a clearly articulate,
cues.zh: 它应该是一个清晰阐述的、

cues.en: articulated vision with a small number of words.
cues.zh: 用少量词语表达清楚的愿景。

cues.en: And the best ideas are usually either
cues.zh: 最好的想法通常要么

cues.en: very different from existing companies
cues.zh: 与现有公司非常不同

cues.en: in one important way. Like Google being a search engine that worked just really well, and none of the other stuff of the portals, or totally new like SpaceX.
cues.zh: 在一个重要方面。比如 Google 是一个就是非常好用的搜索引擎，没有门户网站那些杂七杂八的东西；或者像 SpaceX 那样完全全新。

cues.en: Any company that's a clone of something else that already exists, with some small or made up differentiator,
cues.zh: 任何一家公司，如果只是克隆已经存在的东西，再加一点很小的或编造出来的差异化，

cues.en: like we're gonna be x beautiful design or we're gonna be y for people that like red wine instead.
cues.zh: 比如“我们要做设计很漂亮的 X”，或者“我们要做面向喜欢红酒的人的 Y”。

cues.en: That usually fails.
cues.zh: 这通常会失败。

cues.en: So as I mentioned,
cues.zh: 所以就像我提到的，

cues.en: one of the great things about being a student is that you have a very good perspective on new technology.
cues.zh: 当学生的一大好处是，你能对新技术有很好的视角。

cues.en: And learning to get good at having new ideas takes a while.
cues.zh: 而要学会善于产生新想法，是需要时间的。

cues.en: So start working on that right now.
cues.zh: 所以现在就着手去做吧。

cues.en: That's one thing we hear from people all the time. That they wish they had done more when they were a student.
cues.zh: 这是我们经常听人说的一点：他们希望自己当学生时能多做一些事。

cues.en: The other is meeting potential co founders.
cues.zh: 另一件事是结识潜在的联合创始人。

cues.en: You have no idea how good of an environment you're in right now for meeting people that you can start a company with down the road. And the one thing that we always tell college students is more important than starting any particular start up, is getting to know a lot of potential co founders.
cues.zh: 你根本不知道，现在的环境有多适合结识将来能一起创办公司的人。而我们总是告诉大学生，比创办某一家具体的创业公司更重要的是，去认识很多潜在的联合创始人。

cues.en: So I wanna finish this section of my talk,
cues.zh: 那么我想用一句话来结束演讲的这一部分，

cues.en: with a quote from fifty Cent. This is,
cues.zh: 引用 50 Cent 的一句话。这是，

cues.en: this is from when he was asked about vitamin water.
cues.zh: 这是他当年被问到 Vitaminwater 时说的。

cues.en: I won't read it. It's up there.
cues.zh: 我就不念了，就在上面。

cues.en: But it's about the importance of thinking about what customers want, and thinking about the demands of the market.
cues.zh: 但它讲的是要重视思考客户想要什么，思考市场的需求。

cues.en: Most people don't do this. Most students especially don't do this.
cues.zh: 大多数人都不这么做，尤其是大多数学生。

cues.en: If you can just do this one thing, if you can just learn to think about the market first,
cues.zh: 如果你能做到这一件事，如果你能学会先考虑市场，

cues.en: you will have a big leg up on most people starting startups.
cues.zh: 你就会比大多数创业的人拥有巨大的优势。

cues.en: And this is something,
cues.zh: 还有一点，

cues.en: this is probably the thing that we see wrong with y combinator apps most frequently.
cues.zh: 这大概是我们最常在 Y Combinator 项目里看到的错误。

cues.en: Is that people have not thought about the market first, and what people want first.
cues.zh: 就是人们没有优先考虑市场，也没有优先考虑用户想要什么。

cues.en: So for the next section, I'm gonna talk about building a great product.
cues.zh: 那么接下来这部分，我要讲讲怎么打造一款出色的产品。

cues.en: And here again,
cues.zh: 这里同样，

cues.en: I'm
cues.zh: 我会

cues.en: gonna use a very broad definition of product.
cues.zh: 用非常宽泛的产品定义。

cues.en: It includes customer support and copyright explaining the product. Anything involved in your customer's interaction with what you built from them.
cues.zh: 它包括客户支持、版权说明等对产品的解释，凡是涉及用户与你为他们打造的东西之间互动的内容，都算。

cues.en: To build a really great company, you first have to turn a great idea into a great product. This is really hard, but it's crucially important. And fortunately, it's pretty fun.
cues.zh: 要打造一家真正伟大的公司，首先必须把一个伟大的想法变成一款伟大的产品。这非常难，但至关重要。幸运的是，这也挺有意思。

cues.en: Although great products are always new to the world, and it's hard to give you advice about what to build. There are enough commonalities that we can give you a lot of advice about how to build it.
cues.zh: 尽管伟大的产品对世界来说总是新的，也很难就“该做什么”给你建议。但其中共性足够多，我们可以就“如何打造”给你很多建议。

cues.en: One of the most important tasks for a founder is to make sure that the company builds a great product. Until you've built a great product, almost nothing else matters.
cues.zh: 对创始人来说，最重要的任务之一就是确保公司打造出一款伟大的产品。在你做出伟大产品之前，其他几乎所有事都不重要。

cues.en: When really successful startup founders tell the story of their early days, it's almost always
cues.zh: 那些真正成功的创业公司创始人讲起早期经历时，几乎总是

cues.en: sitting in front of the computer working on their product or talking to their customers.
cues.zh: 坐在电脑前做产品，或者和客户交流。

cues.en: That's pretty much all the time. They do very little else. And you should be very skeptical
cues.zh: 差不多一直如此。它们几乎不做别的。而且你应该非常怀疑。

cues.en: if your time allocation is much different.
cues.zh: 如果你的时间分配差别很大。

cues.en: Most other problems that founders are trying to solve, raising money, getting more press, hiring, business development, etcetera. These are significantly easier when you have a great product.
cues.zh: 创始人要解决的大多数其他问题——融资、获得更多媒体报道、招聘、商务拓展等等——在拥有出色产品时会容易得多。

cues.en: It's really important to take care of that first. Step one is to build something that users love.
cues.zh: 首先把这件事做好非常重要。第一步是做出用户喜爱的产品。

cues.en: At YC, tell we founders to work on their product, talk to users, exercise, eat and sleep, and very little else. All the other stuff I just mentioned, PR conferences, recruiting advisors, doing partnerships.
cues.zh: 在 YC，我们告诉创始人要做产品、和用户交流、锻炼、吃饭睡觉，别的事尽量少做。我刚才提到的那些，公关会议、招聘顾问、做合作。

cues.en: You should ignore all of that and just build a product and then get it as good as possible by talking to your users.
cues.zh: 你应该忽略所有这些，只专注做产品，然后通过与用户交流把它做到尽可能好。

cues.en: Your job is to build something that users love.
cues.zh: 你的任务是做出用户热爱的东西。

cues.en: Very few companies that go on to be super successful get there without first doing this. A lot of good on paper startups fail because they merely make something that people like.
cues.zh: 很少有公司能在没做到这一点的情况下最终获得超级成功。很多纸面上看不错的创业公司会失败，因为它们只是做出了人们喜欢的东西。

cues.en: Making something that people want, but only a medium amount, is a great way to fail and not understand why you're failing. So these are the two jobs.
cues.zh: 做出人们想要、但只是中等程度想要的东西，是失败却又搞不清自己为什么失败的绝佳方式。所以这就是两件事。

cues.en: Something that we say at YC a lot is that it's better to build a small number. It's better to build something that a small number of users love than a large number of users like.
cues.zh: 我们在 YC 经常说，更好的做法是做出数量少、但被一小群用户热爱的东西，而不是做出一大群用户只是喜欢的东西。

cues.en: Of course, it'd be best to build something that a small number of users love. But opportunities
cues.zh: 当然，最好是做出少数用户深爱的东西。但机会

cues.en: to do that for v one are rare, and they're usually not available to start ups. So in practice, you end up choosing either the gray or the orange. You make something that a lot of users like a little bit, or something that a small number of users like, love a lot.
cues.zh: 在 v1 阶段做到这一点的机会很少，而且初创公司通常也轮不到。所以现实中，你最后只能选灰色或橙色。要么做出让很多用户有点喜欢的东西，要么做出让少数用户非常喜爱的东西。

cues.en: And this is a very important piece of advice.
cues.zh: 这是一条非常重要的建议。

cues.en: Build something that a small number of users love.
cues.zh: 做一款让少数用户热爱的东西。

cues.en: It's much easier to expand from something that a small number of people love, to something that a lot of people love,
cues.zh: 从少数人热爱的东西，扩展到让很多人热爱，要容易得多，

cues.en: than from something that a lot of people like, to a lot of people love.
cues.zh: 而从很多人只是喜欢，变成让很多人热爱，则难得多。

cues.en: If you get this right,
cues.zh: 如果这件事做对了，

cues.en: you can get a lot of other things wrong.
cues.zh: 很多其他事情做错也没关系。

cues.en: If you don't get this right, you can get everything else right and you'll probably still fail. So when you start in a startup, this is the only thing you need to care about until it's working.
cues.zh: 如果这件事没做对，即使其他一切都做对，你很可能还是会失败。所以创业初期，在它跑通之前，你唯一需要关心的就是这件事。

cues.en: Sure.
cues.zh: 当然。

cues.en: So you have a choice in a startup. The best thing of all worlds would be to build a product that a lot of people really love.
cues.zh: 所以在创业公司里，你得做个选择。最理想的情况，是做出一个很多人都真正热爱的产品。

cues.en: In practice, you can't usually do that because a big company, if there's an opportunity like that, Google or Facebook will do it. So there's like a limit to the area under the curve of what you can build. And you can either build something that a lot of users like a little bit,
cues.zh: 但现实中，你通常做不到，因为如果有那样的机会，大公司——比如 Google 或 Facebook——就会去做。所以你能构建的东西，其曲线下面积是有限的。你要么做出很多用户有点喜欢的东西，

cues.en: or you can build something that a small number of users love a lot. And like, the total amount of love is the same. It's just a question of how it's distributed.
cues.zh: 要么做出少数用户非常热爱的东西。而且，总的热爱量是一样的。问题只在于它如何分布。

cues.en: And there's like this law of conservation of how much happiness you can put into the world with the first product of a startup.
cues.zh: 有个类似守恒定律的说法：创业公司的第一个产品能给世界带来多少快乐，是守恒的。

cues.en: And so startups always struggle with which of those two they should go. And they seem equal, right? Because the area under the curve is the same.
cues.zh: 所以创业公司总在纠结该走哪条路。它们看起来是等价的，对吧？因为曲线下的面积一样。

cues.en: But we've seen this time and again that they're not. And that it's so much easier to expand.
cues.zh: 但我们一次次看到，它们并不等价。而且扩张要容易得多。

cues.en: Once you've got something that some people love, you can expand that to something that a lot of other people love.
cues.zh: 一旦你做出了让一部分人热爱的东西，就能把它扩展成让很多其他人也热爱的东西。

cues.en: But if you only get ambivalence
cues.zh: 但如果用户只是态度暧昧

cues.en: or sort of like weak enthusiasm
cues.zh: 或者那种微弱的热情

cues.en: and then try to expand that, you'll never get up to a lot of people loving it.
cues.zh: 然后还试图把它扩大，你永远无法让很多人真正爱上它。

cues.en: So the advice is,
cues.zh: 所以建议是，

cues.en: find a small group of users and make them really love what you're doing. Does that make sense?
cues.zh: 找到一小群用户，让他们真正喜欢你做的事。这样说能理解吗？

cues.en: Alright.
cues.zh: 好。

cues.en: One
cues.zh: 一种

cues.en: way that you know when this is working is that you'll get growth by word-of-mouth.
cues.zh: 判断它是否奏效的方法是，你会通过口碑获得增长。

cues.en: If you make something people love,
cues.zh: 如果你做出的东西让人喜爱，

cues.en: people will tell their friends about it. This works for consumer products and enterprise products as well.
cues.zh: 人们会告诉朋友。消费级产品和企业级产品都适用。

cues.en: When people really love something, they tell their friends about it, and you'll see organic growth.
cues.zh: 当人们真心喜欢某个东西时，他们会告诉朋友，你就能看到自然增长。

cues.en: If you find yourself talking about how it's okay that you're not growing,
cues.zh: 如果你发现自己总在说“不增长也没关系”，

cues.en: because there's a big partnership that's gonna come save you or something like that, It's almost always a sign of real trouble.
cues.zh: 因为会有个大合作来拯救你之类的，这几乎总是真正出问题的信号。

cues.en: Sales and marketing are really important, and we're gonna have two classes on them later. But if you don't have some early organic growth, then your product probably isn't good enough yet.
cues.zh: 销售和市场非常重要，我们后面会有两节课专门讲。但如果你没有早期的自然增长，那你的产品可能还不够好。

cues.en: A great product is the secret to long term growth hacking. You should get that right before you worry about anything else. It doesn't get easier to put off making a great product.
cues.zh: 做好产品是长期增长黑客的秘诀。在担心其他任何事情之前，你应该先把这一点做对。拖延打造一款好产品，只会越来越难。

cues.en: If you try to build a growth machine before you have a product that some people really love, you're almost certainly gonna waste your time.
cues.zh: 如果你还没有一款让一些人真正热爱的产品，就想搭建增长机器，那几乎肯定会浪费时间。

cues.en: Breakout companies almost always have a product that's so good that it grows by word-of-mouth.
cues.zh: 爆发式增长的公司几乎总有一款好到能靠口碑传播的产品。

cues.en: Over the long run, great products win.
cues.zh: 从长远来看，好产品会赢。

cues.en: Don't worry about your competitors
cues.zh: 别担心你的竞争对手

cues.en: raising a lot of money and what they may do in the future.
cues.zh: 融了很多钱，或者他们未来可能做什么。

cues.en: They probably aren't very good anyway. Very few startups die from competition.
cues.zh: 反正他们很可能也没那么厉害。很少有创业公司死于竞争。

cues.en: Most die because they themselves fail to make something users love. They spend their time on other things.
cues.zh: 大多数死掉，是因为自己没能做出用户喜爱的东西。他们把时间花在别的事情上。

cues.en: So worry about this
cues.zh: 所以要优先担心这件事

cues.en: above all else.
cues.zh: 胜过其他一切。

cues.en: Another piece of advice to make something that users love, start with something simple.
cues.zh: 另一条建议：要做出用户喜爱的东西，就从简单的东西开始。

cues.en: It's much, much easier to make a great product if you have something simple.
cues.zh: 如果你有一个简单的东西，做出出色的产品会容易得多得多。

cues.en: Even if your eventual plans are super complex, and hopefully they are,
cues.zh: 即使你最终的计划极其复杂——但愿如此——

cues.en: you can almost always start with a smaller subset of the problem than whatever you think is the smallest. And it's hard to build a great product. So you wanna start with as little surface area as possible.
cues.zh: 你几乎总能从比你以为的最小范围还要小的问题子集开始。打造出色产品很难。所以你要从尽可能小的范围开始。

cues.en: Think about the really successful companies and what they started with. Think about products that you really love. They're generally incredibly simple to use and especially to get started using.
cues.zh: 想想那些真正成功的公司，以及它们起步时做的是什么。想想你真正喜欢的产品。它们通常用起来极其简单，尤其是上手使用。

cues.en: The first version of Facebook was almost comically simple.
cues.zh: Facebook 的第一个版本简单得几乎有点可笑。

cues.en: The first version of Google was just an ugly web page with a text box and two buttons. But it returned the best results and that's why users loved it. The iPhone is far simpler to use than any smartphone that ever came before it, and it was the first one that people really loved.
cues.zh: Google 的第一个版本只是一个丑陋的网页，上面有一个文本框和两个按钮。但它返回的结果最好，所以用户喜欢它。iPhone 用起来比之前任何智能手机都简单得多，也是第一款真正让人们喜爱的手机。

cues.en: Another reason that simple's good is because it forces you to do one thing extremely well. And you have to do that to make something that people love.
cues.zh: 简单之所以好，另一个原因是它会迫使你把一件事做到极致。而你必须这样做，才能做出人们喜爱的东西。

cues.en: The word fanatical comes up again and again when you listen to successful founders talk about how they think about their product.
cues.zh: 听成功创始人谈论他们如何思考产品时，“狂热”这个词会反复出现。

cues.en: Founders talk about being fanatical in the way they care about the quality of the small details.
cues.zh: 创始人们会谈到，他们对小细节质量的在意近乎狂热。

cues.en: Fanatical in getting the copy that they use to explain the product just right. And fanatical in the way they think about customer support.
cues.zh: 对用来解释产品的文案，他们追求恰到好处，近乎狂热；对客户支持的思考方式也同样狂热。

cues.en: In fact, one thing that correlates with success among the YC companies is the founders that hook up PagerDuty to their ticketing system. So that even if a user emails in the middle of the night when the founders are asleep, they still get a response within an hour.
cues.zh: 事实上，在 YC 公司中，与成功相关的一个因素是：创始人把 PagerDuty 接入他们的工单系统。这样即使用户在半夜创始人睡着时发邮件，用户仍能在一小时内得到回复。

cues.en: Companies actually do this in the early days. These founders feel physical pain when the product sucks and they wanna wake up and fix it. They don't ship crap, and if they do, they fix it very, very quickly.
cues.zh: 很多公司在早期确实会这样做。这些创始人看到产品烂会感到生理上的痛苦，他们想一醒来就去修好它。他们不会发布垃圾，如果真发布了，也会非常非常快地修好。

cues.en: And it definitely takes some level of fanaticism
cues.zh: 而这确实需要一定程度的狂热

cues.en: to build a great product.
cues.zh: 才能做出伟大的产品。

cues.en: You need some users to help with the feedback cycle. But the way to get those users is manually. You should go recruit them by hand. Don't do things like buy Google ads in the early days to get initial users. You don't need very many. You just need ones that will give you feedback every day and eventually love your product.
cues.zh: 你需要一些用户来帮助完成反馈循环。但获得这些用户的方式是手工的。你应该亲手去招募他们。早期不要做买 Google 广告之类的事来获取初始用户。你不需要很多用户，你只需要那些每天都会给你反馈、并最终会爱上你产品的用户。

cues.en: So instead of trying to get them on Google AdWords, just find a few people in the world that will be good users. Recruit them by hand.
cues.zh: 所以与其琢磨着去投 Google AdWords，不如直接在全球找几个合适的使用者，亲手把他们招进来。

cues.en: Ben Silverman,
cues.zh: Ben Silverman，

cues.en: when everyone thought Pinterest was a joke, recruited the initial Pinterest users by tagging up strangers in coffee shops. He really did. He just walked around Palo Alto and said, will you please use my product?
cues.zh: 当所有人都觉得 Pinterest 是个笑话时，他靠在咖啡店里搭讪陌生人，招来了 Pinterest 最早的一批用户。他真的这么干了。他就在 Palo Alto 到处转，问人家：你愿意用用我的产品吗？

cues.en: He also used to run around the Apple store in Palo Alto. And he would like settle the browsers to the Pinterest homepage real quick before they caught him and kicked him out.
cues.zh: 他还常跑到 Palo Alto 的 Apple store 里，趁店员发现、把他赶出去之前，飞快地把浏览器设成 Pinterest 的主页。

cues.en: So then when people walked in there, they're like, oh, what is this?
cues.zh: 所以当人们走进那里时，他们会说，哦，这是什么？

cues.en: This is an important example of doing things that don't scale.
cues.zh: 这是一个重要的例子，说明要做那些无法规模化的事情。

cues.en: If you haven't read Paul Graham's essay on that topic, you definitely should.
cues.zh: 如果你还没读过 Paul Graham 关于这个主题的文章，那你一定要读一读。

cues.en: So get users manually and remember that the goal is to get a small group of them to love you. Understand that group extremely well. Get extremely close into them, close to them. Listen to them and you'll almost always find out that they're very willing to give you feedback.
cues.zh: 所以要手动获取用户，并记住目标是让一小群用户爱上你。要极其深入地了解这群人。要极其贴近他们、靠近他们。倾听他们，你几乎总会发现，他们非常愿意给你反馈。

cues.en: Even if you're building the product for yourself, listen to outside users and they'll tell you how to make a product they'll pay for.
cues.zh: 即便产品是给自己做的，也要倾听外部用户，他们会告诉你怎样做出他们愿意付费的产品。

cues.en: Do whatever you need to make them love you and make them know what you're doing because they're also gonna be the advocates that help you get your next users.
cues.zh: 尽一切努力让他们喜欢你、让他们知道你在做什么，因为他们也会成为帮你带来下一批用户的拥护者。

cues.en: You wanna build an engine in the company that transforms feedback from users into product decisions.
cues.zh: 你要在公司里建立一套机制，把用户反馈转化为产品决策。

cues.en: Then get it back in front of the users and repeat.
cues.zh: 然后把成果拿回用户面前，如此循环往复。

cues.en: Ask them what they like and what they don't like and watch them use it.
cues.zh: 问问他们喜欢什么、不喜欢什么，然后看着他们用。

cues.en: Ask them what they pay for.
cues.zh: 问问他们为什么付费。

cues.en: Ask them if they'd be really bummed if your company went away.
cues.zh: 问问他们，如果你的公司没了，他们会不会真的很不爽。

cues.en: Ask them what would make them recommend the product to their friends. And ask them if they've recommended it to any yet.
cues.zh: 问问他们，什么会让他们把产品推荐给朋友。再问问他们，到现在有没有推荐过。

cues.en: You should make this feedback loop as tight as possible. If your product gets 10% better every week, that compounds really, really quickly. One
cues.zh: 你应该让这个反馈闭环尽可能紧凑。如果你的产品每周提升 10%，复利效应会非常非常快。软件创业公司

cues.en: of the great advantages of start, of software startups is just how short you can make the feedback loop. It can be measured in hours. And the best companies usually have the tightest feedback loops.
cues.zh: 的巨大优势之一，就是你能把反馈闭环做得多短。它可以以小时计。而最好的公司通常拥有最紧凑的反馈闭环。

cues.en: You should try to keep this going for all of your company's life, but it's really important in the early days.
cues.zh: 这件事你应该在整个公司生命周期里坚持做，但在早期尤其重要。

cues.en: The good news is that all of this is doable. It's hard. It takes a lot of effort, but there's no magic. The plan is at least straightforward and you will eventually get to a great product.
cues.zh: 好消息是，这一切都可行。它很难，需要大量投入，但没有什么魔法。至少计划是清晰的，你最终会做出很棒的产品。

cues.en: Great founders don't put anyone between themselves and their users.
cues.zh: 优秀的创始人不会在自己和用户之间放任何人。

cues.en: The founders of these companies do things like sales and customer support themselves in the early days. It's critical to get this loop embedded in the culture. In fact, the specific problem that we always see with Stanford startups for some reason, is that the students try and hire sales and customer support people right away. And you've got to do this yourself. It's the only way.
cues.zh: 这些公司的创始人在早期会亲自做销售和客户支持之类的事。把这一闭环融入公司文化至关重要。事实上，不知为何，我们在斯坦福创业公司身上总能看到一个具体问题：学生们总想立刻招销售和客户支持人员。你必须亲自做这些事。这是唯一的方法。

cues.en: You really need to use metrics to keep yourself honest on this.
cues.zh: 你真的需要用指标来让自己在这件事上保持诚实。

cues.en: It really is true that the company will build whatever the CEO decides to measure.
cues.zh: 公司真的会去做 CEO 决定衡量的那些事，这一点千真万确。

cues.en: If you're building an internet service, ignore things like total registrations. Don't talk about them. Don't let anyone in the company talk about them. And look at growth in active users, activity levels, cohort retention, revenue, net promoter scores, these things that matter. And then be brutally honest if they aren't going in the right direction. Startups live on growth. It's the indicator of a great product.
cues.zh: 如果你在做互联网服务，就别管总注册数这类指标。别谈它们，也别让公司里任何人谈它们。要看活跃用户的增长、活跃度、同期群留存、收入、净推荐值，这些才是真正重要的东西。然后，如果它们没有朝正确的方向发展，就要极其诚实地面对。创业公司靠增长活着，增长是伟大产品的标志。

cues.en: So this about wraps up the overview on building a great product. I wanna emphasize again that if you don't get this right, nothing else we talk about in the class will matter.
cues.zh: 好，关于打造优秀产品的概述到这里就差不多讲完了。我想再次强调，如果这一点做不好，我们在课上讲的其它一切都没有意义。

cues.en: You can basically ignore everything else that we talk about until this is working well.
cues.zh: 基本上，在这件事做好之前，你可以忽略我们讲的其它所有内容。

cues.en: On the positive side, this is one of the most fun parts of building a startup. So I'm gonna pause here. I'll pick back up with the rest of this on Thursday. And now we're gonna have Dustin talk about,
cues.zh: 好的一面是，这是创办创业公司最有意思的部分之一。所以我先在这里停一下，周四再接着讲剩下的内容。接下来我们请 Dustin 来讲，

cues.en: why you should start a startup.
cues.zh: 为什么你应该去创业。

cues.en: Thank you for coming Dustin. Sure.
cues.zh: 谢谢你过来，Dustin。当然。

cues.en: But yeah, so Sam asked me to talk about
cues.zh: 不过，Sam 让我来谈谈

cues.en: why you should start a startup. There's a bunch of reasons you might have.
cues.zh: 为什么你应该创业。你可能有很多理由。

cues.en: And there's a bunch of common reasons that people have that I hear all the time for for why you might start a startup.
cues.zh: 大家常说的、我经常听到的创业理由有一大堆。

cues.en: It's important to know like, what reason is yours. Because some of them only make sense in, in certain contexts.
cues.zh: 重要的是搞清楚，你的理由是什么。因为有些理由只在特定情境下才成立。

cues.en: Some of them will actually like lead you astray. You may have been misled by the way that
cues.zh: 有些理由其实会让你误入歧途。你可能被这种叙事误导了：

cues.en: Hollywood or the press likes to romanticize entrepreneurship.
cues.zh: 好莱坞或媒体喜欢把创业浪漫化。

cues.en: So I wanna try and like, illuminate
cues.zh: 所以我想试着说明一下

cues.en: you know, some of those potential fallacies so you guys can can make the decision in a clear way.
cues.zh: 你们也知道，其中一些潜在的谬误，好让你们能更清楚地做决定。

cues.zh: 然后我会讲讲我最喜欢的、真正去创业的理由。它和 Sam 刚才讲的很多内容密切相关。但意外的是，我觉得它并不是最常见的原因。通常人们是出于其他原因之一。

cues.en: Or they just wanna start up, you know, start a company for the sake of starting a company. So
cues.zh: 或者他们只是想创业，你知道，为了开公司而开公司。所以

cues.en: the, the four common reasons just to enumerate them are, it's glamorous.
cues.zh: 四个常见原因，逐一列举的话就是：它很光鲜。

cues.en: You know, you'll be, you'll get to be the boss.
cues.zh: 你知道，你会，你会成为老板。

cues.en: You'll have flexibility,
cues.zh: 你会有灵活性，

cues.en: especially over your schedule.
cues.zh: 尤其是在日程安排上。

cues.en: And you'll have the chance to have, you know, bigger impact and make more money than you, than you might by joining a later stage company.
cues.zh: 而且你有机会产生更大的影响、赚更多的钱，比你去加入后期阶段的公司可能得到的更多。

cues.en: So, okay. So
cues.zh: 所以，好。那么

cues.en: you know, you, you guys are probably pretty familiar with this concept. When I wrote the medium post, which a lot of you guys read a year ago,
cues.zh: 你们可能对这个概念挺熟悉的。一年前我写了那篇 Medium 文章，你们很多人都读过，

cues.en: I felt like the story in the press was a little more unbalanced.
cues.zh: 我觉得媒体报道里的说法有点失衡。

cues.en: You know, entrepreneurship just got romanticized quite a bit. You know, the movie The Social Network came out. Had a lot of sort of like, bad aspects of of, you know, what it's like to be an entrepreneur. But mainly sort of painted this picture of like, there's a lot of partying, and you just kinda moved from like, brilliant insight to another brilliant insight.
cues.zh: 你知道吗，创业这件事最近被浪漫化得有点过头了。电影《社交网络》上映之后，其实里面也展现了不少创业中糟糕的一面，但主要还是塑造了这样一种画面：有没完没了的派对，而你就这么从一个绝妙的想法跳到另一个绝妙的想法。

cues.en: And really made it, you know, seem like this like really cool thing to do.
cues.zh: 而且真的让它看起来像是一件特别酷的事。

cues.en: And I think the reality
cues.zh: 而我觉得现实情况

cues.en: is just, you know, not quite so glamorous. There's sort of a, there's an ugly side to being an entrepreneur.
cues.zh: 其实，你知道，并没那么光鲜。创业还有某种……不那么好看的一面。

cues.en: And also just more importantly what what you're actually spending your time on is, is just a lot of hard work. Sam mentioned this, but you're basically just sitting at your desk, heads down, focused
cues.zh: 更重要的是，你实际花时间做的事，就是大量辛苦的工作。Sam 提到过这一点，但你基本上就是坐在桌前，埋头专注地

cues.en: answering customer customer support emails, doing sales, figuring out hard engineering problems.
cues.zh: 回复客户支持邮件、做销售、解决棘手的工程问题。

cues.en: So it's really important that you kind of like go in with, with eyes wide open. And then also it's, it's really quite stressful. And this has been a popular topic in the press lately.
cues.zh: 所以，你务必睁大眼睛、认清现实再入场，这真的很重要。而且这压力确实非常大。最近媒体也一直在热议这个话题。

cues.en: The Economist actually ran a story just last week called like Entrepreneur's Anonymous. And shows like a founder kinda like hiding under his desk and talking about like founder depression.
cues.zh: The Economist 上周还真发了一篇报道，标题类似《创业者匿名互助会》。里面写到有个创始人躲在桌子底下，聊着“创始人抑郁”之类的事。

cues.en: So this is like a very real thing. Like, you know, let's be real. This, if you start a company, it's gonna be extremely hard.
cues.zh: 所以这是非常真实的事。你知道，咱们现实点说，如果你去创业，那会极其艰难。

cues.en: Why is it so stressful? So a couple reasons.
cues.zh: 为什么压力这么大？有几个原因。

cues.en: One is you've got a lot of responsibility.
cues.zh: 一是你背负着很多责任。

cues.en: So, people in any kind of career
cues.zh: 所以，无论从事什么职业的人

cues.en: have fear of failure. It's kind of just like a dominant part of the psychology.
cues.zh: 都会害怕失败。这几乎是心理中很主导的一部分。

cues.en: But when you're an entrepreneur, you have fear of failure on behalf of yourself and all of the people who decided to follow you. So that's really stressful.
cues.zh: 但作为创业者，你不仅为自己害怕失败，也为所有决定跟随你的人害怕失败。所以压力真的很大。

cues.en: In some cases, these people are depending on you for their livelihood. Even when that's not true, they've decided to devote the the best of your years of their life to following you. And so you're responsible for the opportunity cost of their time. So that's a big deal.
cues.zh: 有些情况下，这些人靠你维持生计。即使并非如此，他们也决定把人生中最好的年华用来追随你。所以你要为他们的时间机会成本负责。这可不是小事。

cues.en: And you're always on call if something comes up.
cues.zh: 而且一旦有事，你总是随时待命。

cues.en: Maybe not always at three in the morning, but for some startups that's true. But if something important comes up, you're gonna deal with it. That's kind of the end of the story. Doesn't matter if you're on vacation. Doesn't matter if it's the weekend.

cues.zh: 他们有现成的庞大用户群。比如 Facebook，有十亿用户。或者 Google，也有十亿用户。

cues.en: They have existing infrastructure you get to build on. That's also increasingly true for new start ups. Things like AWS and all these like awesome
cues.zh: 他们有现成的基础设施，你可以基于它来构建。对初创公司来说，这一点也越来越普遍。比如 AWS，以及所有这些很棒的

cues.en: independent service providers.
cues.zh: 独立服务提供商。

cues.en: But you usually get some like proprietor proprietary technology and it's all maintained for you. It's a pretty great place to start. And you get to work with a team and they'll help you just leverage your idea into something great. So a couple specific examples.
cues.zh: 但通常你能接触到一些专有技术，而且这些都有人帮你维护。这是个很不错的起点。你还能和团队一起工作，他们会帮你把想法变成很棒的东西。举几个具体例子。

cues.en: Brett Taylor came into employee around, or came into Google as around employee number 1,500.
cues.zh: Brett Taylor 加入 Google 时大约是第 1,500 号员工。

cues.en: And he invented Google Maps. This is a product you guys probably use every day. I used it to get here.
cues.zh: 他发明了 Google Maps。这个产品你们可能每天都在用。我就是靠它找到这儿的。

cues.en: And it's used by hundreds of millions of people all around the world. Didn't need to start a company to do that. Did happen to get a big financial reward. But the, the point is you had massive impact.
cues.zh: 全世界有数亿人在用它。这并不需要去创办一家公司。倒是确实拿到了很大的财务回报。但重点是，你产生了巨大的影响力。

cues.en: My co founder Justin Rosenstein
cues.zh: 我的联合创始人 Justin Rosenstein

cues.en: joined Google a little later after Brett.
cues.zh: 在 Brett 之后稍晚一些加入了 Google。

cues.en: He was a PM there.
cues.zh: 他在那儿做产品经理。

cues.en: And just as a side project, he ended up prototyping
cues.zh: 他最初只是把它当副业项目，最后做出了原型

cues.en: chat, which used, which used to be a stand alone app
cues.zh: 聊天功能，它曾经是一个独立应用

cues.en: as integrated into Gmail, like you see it in the upper right there.
cues.zh: 后来被整合进了 Gmail，就像你在右上角看到的那样。

cues.en: And before he did that, like people didn't even think you could do chat over Ajax or chat in the browser at all. And he just kind of like demonstrated it and showed it to his team and then they made it happen. And again, this is, this is probably a product most of you use maybe every day.
cues.zh: 在他做这件事之前，人们甚至根本不认为你能用 Ajax 做聊天，或者在浏览器里聊天。他只是把它做出来演示了一下，展示给团队看，然后他们就把它实现了。再说一次，这可能是你们大多数人几乎每天都会用的产品。

cues.en: And then perhaps even more impressively, shortly after that, JR left. He became employee round number two fifty at Facebook.
cues.zh: 然后或许更令人惊叹的是，在那之后不久，JR 就离开了。他成了 Facebook 的第 250 号员工。

cues.en: And he led a hackathon project along with people like Andrew Bosworth and Leah Perlman
cues.zh: 他和 Andrew Bosworth、Leah Perlman 等人一起带了个黑客松项目

cues.en: to create the like button. So this is one of the most popular elements anywhere on the web. Totally changes how people use it. And again, didn't need to start a company to do it. And almost certainly would have failed if he had tried, because he really needed the distribution of Facebook to make it work.
cues.zh: 做出了点赞按钮。这是全网最受欢迎的元素之一，彻底改变了人们的使用方式。再说一次，做这个不需要去创办公司。而且如果他去创业，几乎肯定会失败，因为他真的需要 Facebook 的分发能力才能做成。

cues.en: So important to, to keep in mind the context for
cues.zh: 所以要牢记你所处的环境，

cues.en: what kind of company you're trying to start and like,
cues.zh: 想清楚你要创办的是什么类型的公司，

cues.en: where will you actually be able to make it happen.
cues.zh: 以及你到底能在哪里把它做成。

cues.zh: 那么最好的理由是什么？

cues.zh: Sam 已经稍微聊过这个了。不过

cues.en: basically, you can't not do it. You're super passionate about this idea. You're the right person to do it. You've gotta make it happen.
cues.zh: 基本上，你就是没法不做。你对这个想法特别有热情。你就是做这件事的合适人选。你必须把它做成。

cues.en: So how does this break down?
cues.zh: 那么这怎么拆解呢？

cues.zh: 完美。

cues.en: So
cues.zh: 那么

cues.en: this this is sort of like a word play. You can't not do it in two ways. One is, you're so passionate about it that you just like, you have to do it. You're gonna do it anyway.
cues.zh: 这这有点像文字游戏。“你不能不做”有两层意思。一是你对它太有热情了，以至于你就是非做不可。反正你都会去做。

cues.en: And this is really important because you'll need that passion to get through all of those like hard parts of being an entrepreneur that we talked about earlier. You'll also need it to effectively recruit. Candidates can smell when you don't have passion. And there are enough entrepreneurs out there who do have passion that they may as well work for one of those. So this is sort of like table stakes for being an entrepreneur.
cues.zh: 这真的很重要，因为你需要那份热情，才能熬过我们之前聊过的创业者的那些艰难时刻。你也需要它来有效招聘。候选人能察觉到你没有热情。而且外面有足够多有热情的创业者，他们完全可以选择为其中一位工作。所以这算是成为创业者的基本门槛。

cues.en: Your subconscious can also tell when you don't have passion, and that'll be a huge problem.
cues.zh: 你的潜意识也能察觉到你没有热情，那会是个大问题。

cues.en: And then, so the other way to interpret this is the world needs you to do it. So this is sort of validation that the idea is important. It's gonna make the world better. So the world needs it.
cues.zh: 然后，另一种解读方式是：世界需要你去做这件事。所以这算是一种验证，说明这个想法很重要。它会让世界变得更好。所以世界需要它。

cues.en: If it's not if it's not something the world needs, go do something the world needs. Your time's really valuable. There are plenty of good ideas out there. Maybe it's not one of your own. Maybe it's an existing company. But you may as well work on something that's gonna be good.
cues.zh: 如果它不是世界需要的东西，那就去做世界需要的事。你的时间非常宝贵。外面有很多好想法。也许它不是你自己的。也许它是一家现有公司。但你不如去做一些真正会变好的事情。

cues.en: And then the second way to interpret this is the world needs you to do it. You're actually well suited to this problem in some way.
cues.zh: 然后第二种解读方式是，这个世界需要你去做这件事。你在某种程度上其实很适合解决这个问题。

cues.en: If this isn't true,
cues.zh: 如果这一点不成立，

cues.en: it may be a sign that
cues.zh: 那可能说明

cues.en: your time is better spent somewhere else. But also just best case scenario, if this isn't true, you out compete the team for which it is true. And you just end up with like a sub optimal outcome for the world. That doesn't feel very good. So drawing this back to my own experience.
cues.zh: 你的时间花在别处会更好。而且往最好的情况说，如果这一点不成立，你却在竞争中胜过了真正适合这件事的团队，最终只会让世界得到一个次优的结果。这感觉可不太好。那么回到我自己的经历。

cues.en: At Asana, you know, Justin and I were kind of like reluctant entrepreneurs.
cues.zh: 在 Asana，你知道，Justin 和我算是有点勉为其难的创业者。

cues.en: We...
cues.zh: 我们……

cues.en: Before we founded Asana. So we were working at Facebook. We were already working on a great problem.
cues.zh: 在我们创办 Asana 之前。那时我们在 Facebook 工作。我们手上已经有一个很棒的课题。

cues.en: And we would basically work all day long on our normal projects. And then at night, we would keep working on this internal task manager
cues.zh: 基本上我们白天一整天都在做自己的常规项目。然后到了晚上，我们继续做这个内部任务管理器，

cues.en: that was used internally at the company. And it was just because we were like so passionate about the idea. It was so clearly valuable that we couldn't do anything else.
cues.zh: 它是公司内部在用的。之所以这样，就是因为我们太热爱这个想法了。它明显太有价值了，我们根本没法去做别的事。

cues.en: And at some point, we had to have the hard conversation of like, okay, well what does it mean if we don't actually start this company? We're pretty, we're able to see the impact it was having on Facebook. We're pretty convinced it could be really valuable for the world. We're also pretty convinced nobody else was gonna build it. The problem had been around a long time and we just kept seeing sort of incremental solutions to it. So if we didn't go out with the one that we thought was best, we thought there'd be a lot of value left on the table.
cues.zh: 后来到了某个节点，我们不得不进行一场艰难的对话：好吧，如果我们真的不创办这家公司，那意味着什么？我们很清楚地看到它在 Facebook 上产生的影响。我们很确信它对世界会非常有价值。我们也很确信不会有别人去把它做出来。这个问题已经存在很久了，而我们一直看到的都是一些渐进式的解决方案。所以，如果我们不推出自己认为最好的那个方案，我们觉得会有很多价值被白白错失。

cues.en: And,
cues.zh: 而且，

cues.en: yeah. So we just couldn't couldn't stop working on it. And literally the idea was like beating itself out of our chest, like forcing itself into the world. And I think that's the feeling you should really be looking for when you start a company. That's how you know you have the right idea.
cues.zh: 对。我们就是停不下来，没法不去做它。毫不夸张地说，这个想法简直像要从胸口蹦出来，硬要闯进这个世界。我觉得，这就是你创业时真正该寻找的感觉。这样你才知道自己抓住了对的想法。
